guide.title: Unit 2: Interactions Among Branches of Government: review guide
guide.intro: This unit, the most heavily weighted on the exam, covers how Congress, the president, the courts, and the bureaucracy use and check power. Required documents include Federalist No. 70 (on a single, energetic executive) and Federalist No. 78 (on the judiciary); the required case is Marbury v. Madison (1803).

sections.title: Congress
body: The House (435 members, two-year terms, seats by population) and the Senate (100 members, six-year terms, two per state) share lawmaking but differ in rules. The House uses a Rules Committee to limit debate; the Senate allows unlimited debate, so a filibuster can block a bill unless 60 senators vote for cloture. Most bills die in committee.

Congress has enumerated powers (taxing, spending, regulating commerce, declaring war) and implied powers through the Necessary and Proper Clause. Members act as delegates (following constituents' views), trustees (using their own judgment), or politicos (mixing both). Divided government and partisanship often produce gridlock.
points: Know at least one difference in House and Senate rules.

sections.title: The presidency
body: Formal powers include the veto, commander in chief, treaty making (with two-thirds Senate approval), and appointments (with Senate confirmation). Informal powers include executive orders, executive agreements, signing statements, and the bully pulpit of public communication. Federalist No. 70 argued that a single executive brings energy and decisiveness to government.

Congress checks the president through veto overrides (two-thirds of each house), confirmation, the power of the purse, impeachment, and the War Powers Resolution of 1973, which requires presidents to notify Congress after sending troops and to withdraw them within 60 days without congressional approval (plus 30 days to withdraw).
points: Presidents expand power through executive orders and agreements.

sections.title: The federal courts
body: In Marbury v. Madison (1803) the Court established judicial review, the power to strike down laws and actions that violate the Constitution. Federal judges serve during good behavior (effectively for life), which Federalist No. 78 defended as protecting judicial independence; Hamilton called the judiciary the “least dangerous” branch.

Courts generally follow precedent (stare decisis). Judicial restraint means deferring to elected branches; judicial activism means a willingness to overturn their decisions. The other branches check the courts through appointments, confirmation, changes to the courts' jurisdiction, constitutional amendments, and by passing new laws.
points: Judicial review comes from Marbury, not the text of the Constitution.
Know at least two checks on the courts.

sections.title: The bureaucracy
body: The federal bureaucracy includes cabinet departments, independent regulatory commissions, independent executive agencies such as the Environmental Protection Agency, and government corporations. Congress often passes broad laws and leaves details to agencies, which use discretionary and rulemaking authority to write regulations.

Congress oversees the bureaucracy through committee hearings and the power of the purse; the president through appointments and executive orders; courts through review of agency rules. Iron triangles link an agency, a congressional committee, and an interest group with shared interests; issue networks are looser webs of experts and advocates. The merit-based civil service began with the Pendleton Act of 1883.
points: Rulemaking authority is delegated by Congress.
Oversight tools include hearings, budgets, appointments, and lawsuits.

example.prompt: Explain one way Congress can respond if it disagrees with how an agency is enforcing a law.
example.solution: Congress can hold oversight hearings to question agency officials, cut or condition the agency's funding (the power of the purse), or pass a new law that changes the agency's authority.

misconceptions: “A filibuster can happen in the House.”
House rules limit debate; the filibuster is a Senate practice.
“Executive orders are laws passed by Congress.”
They direct the executive branch and can be overturned by courts or later presidents.
Judicial review was established by the Court in Marbury v. Madison.
Most are civil servants hired on merit; top officials are appointed.

passages.title: Source A: The Constitution, Article II, Section 2
text: “The President shall be Commander in Chief of the Army and Navy of the United States, and of the Militia of the several States, when called into the actual Service of the United States . . . He shall have Power, by and with the Advice and Consent of the Senate, to make Treaties, provided two thirds of the Senators present concur; and he shall nominate, and by and with the Advice and Consent of the Senate, shall appoint Ambassadors, other public Ministers and Consuls, Judges of the supreme Court, and all other Officers of the United States, whose Appointments are not herein otherwise provided for”
passages.attribution: The U.S. Constitution, Article II, Section 2 (1787). Public domain. Wording follows the text printed in OpenStax American Government 4e, Appendix B.
passages.licenseOrRights: The original text is in the public domain (the U.S. Constitution, a public document adopted in 1787 and amended since). StudySprint quotes it as printed in OpenStax American Government 4e (openstax.org/books/american-government-4e/pages/b-the-constitution-of-the-united-states); no OpenStax commentary is copied.

questions.prompt: According to Source A, which presidential power requires approval by two-thirds of the senators present?
choices: Commanding the military
Nominating Supreme Court justices
Appointing ambassadors
Making treaties
questions.explanation: The excerpt says treaties require that “two thirds of the Senators present concur.”
choiceExplanations: The excerpt names the president commander in chief without requiring Senate approval.
Justices are nominated by the president and confirmed by majority Senate vote.
Appointments need Senate consent, but by majority vote, not two-thirds.

questions.prompt: The Senate's role in confirming judges and officials, described in Source A, is best understood as
choices: a power that lets the Senate choose its own nominees
a way for the states to approve each federal appointment
a legislative check on the president's appointment power
a judicial check on the Senate's power to make laws
questions.explanation: Requiring Senate consent lets the legislative branch limit whom the president can appoint.
choiceExplanations: The president nominates; the Senate can only approve or reject.
Senators vote, not the state governments.
Confirmation is a Senate power over the executive, not a court power.

questions.prompt: Presidents often make executive agreements with other countries instead of treaties mainly because executive agreements
choices: require the approval of both houses of Congress
must be approved by the Supreme Court before they can take effect
are permanent and can't be changed by later presidents
don't require the two-thirds Senate approval described in Source A
questions.explanation: Executive agreements avoid the treaty ratification process, which expands presidential power in foreign affairs.
choiceExplanations: Avoiding congressional approval is the point; they don't require both houses.
The Court doesn't approve agreements in advance.
Later presidents can change or end executive agreements.

questions.prompt: Alexander Hamilton argued in Federalist No. 70 that good government needs an energetic executive. This argument most directly supports which feature in Source A?
choices: A list of offices filled by appointment
Senate approval of treaties by a two-thirds vote
A single president serving as commander in chief
Senate confirmation of Supreme Court justices
questions.explanation: Hamilton argued that a single executive can act with decision and speed, as a unified commander in chief can.
choiceExplanations: The list of appointments describes how offices are filled, not why one executive is needed.
Senate approval of treaties limits executive energy rather than supplying it.
Confirmation is a check on the executive, not a source of energy.

questions.prompt: Based on Source B, at which stage did the largest number of bills fail to advance?
choices: Between passing the House and passing the Senate as well
Between committee and passing the House
Between introduction and being reported out of committee
Between passing the Senate and becoming law
questions.explanation: The number fell from 10,000 introduced to 900 reported out of committee, a drop of 9,100 bills.
choiceExplanations: That drop was 350 bills (700 to 350).
That drop was 200 bills (900 to 700).
That drop was 100 bills (350 to 250).

questions.prompt: Which feature of Congress best explains the pattern at the first stage in Source B?
choices: Committees and their chairs decide which bills get hearings and votes
The Supreme Court reviews each bill before it reaches committee
Senators may filibuster bills while they are still in committee
The president must sign each bill before any committee can consider it
questions.explanation: Committees screen legislation, and most bills are never taken up, so they die in committee.
choiceExplanations: Courts review laws after enactment, not bills in committee.
Filibusters occur on the Senate floor, not in committee.
Presidents sign bills only after both houses pass them.

questions.prompt: Which Senate rule could help explain why fewer bills passed the Senate than the House in Source B?
choices: Equal representation, which requires that senators vote unanimously
Unlimited debate, which lets a filibuster block a vote unless 60 senators end it
The requirement that each Senate bill be approved by the president before a vote
The Rules Committee, which sets strict time limits on floor debate
questions.explanation: The filibuster and the 60-vote cloture rule make it harder to bring bills to a final vote in the Senate.
choiceExplanations: Equal representation doesn't require unanimous votes.
Presidential approval comes after congressional passage.
The Rules Committee is a House institution that speeds bills along.

questions.prompt: Which is the most important limitation of Source B for judging how productive Congress was?
choices: It shows only Senate actions and leaves out the House
It counts bills without showing how important or far-reaching each one was
It reports percentages instead of the actual number of bills in each stage
It includes bills that were never introduced in Congress
questions.explanation: A count treats a major budget law and a minor renaming bill the same, so it can't show how much Congress accomplished.
choiceExplanations: The table includes House passage.
It reports numbers, not percentages.
It begins with bills that were introduced.

questions.prompt: How can Congress override a presidential veto?
choices: By asking the Supreme Court to declare the veto unconstitutional
By a three-fourths vote of the state legislatures
By a two-thirds vote in both the House and the Senate
By a simple majority vote in the House of Representatives
questions.explanation: Article I requires two-thirds of each house to override a veto.
choiceExplanations: Vetoes are overridden by Congress, not courts.
State legislatures ratify amendments; they don't override vetoes.
A simple majority in one house isn't enough.

questions.prompt: An executive order is best described as
choices: a directive managing the executive branch that later presidents can reverse
a law passed by Congress at the request of the president
a court ruling that interprets the president's powers
a treaty made with another nation without the Senate's approval or debate
questions.explanation: Executive orders direct federal agencies and carry legal force, but courts can strike them down and later presidents can revoke them.
choiceExplanations: Laws are passed by Congress; executive orders come from the president.
Court rulings come from the judicial branch.
Agreements with other nations are executive agreements, not orders.

questions.prompt: The War Powers Resolution of 1973 was intended mainly to
choices: transfer command of the military from the president to Congress during any war
limit how long presidents can keep troops in combat without congressional approval
give the president sole power to declare war on other nations
require Supreme Court approval before troops are sent abroad
questions.explanation: It requires the president to notify Congress after deploying troops and to withdraw them within 60 days (with 30 more to withdraw) unless Congress authorizes the action.
choiceExplanations: The president remains commander in chief.
The Constitution gives Congress, not the president, the power to declare war.
The courts play no approval role under the law.

questions.prompt: Marbury v. Madison (1803) is significant because it established
choices: the Supreme Court's power of judicial review
Congress's power to create lower federal courts
the right of states to nullify federal laws
the president's power to appoint federal judges
questions.explanation: Marshall's opinion held that the Court can strike down laws that conflict with the Constitution.
choiceExplanations: Congress's power to create lower courts comes from Article III.
Marbury didn't address state nullification.
The appointment power comes from Article II, not Marbury.

questions.prompt: Federal judges serve “during good Behaviour,” effectively for life. The main purpose of this arrangement is to
choices: make the judiciary the most powerful of the three branches
ensure that judges follow the wishes of the voters as shown in each election
allow the president to remove judges whose decisions he dislikes
protect judges from political pressure so they can rule independently
questions.explanation: Federalist No. 78 argued that permanent tenure keeps judges independent of the elected branches.
choiceExplanations: Hamilton called the judiciary the “least dangerous” branch.
Life tenure insulates judges from elections rather than tying them to voters.
Presidents can't remove judges; only impeachment can.

questions.prompt: A court that decides a case by following an earlier decision on the same legal question is applying
choices: senatorial courtesy
judicial activism
stare decisis
original jurisdiction
questions.explanation: Stare decisis (“let the decision stand”) means following precedent.
choiceExplanations: Senatorial courtesy concerns the confirmation of judges in a senator's state.
Activism means a willingness to overturn the elected branches' decisions.
Original jurisdiction is a court's power to hear a case first.

questions.prompt: A justice who usually defers to Congress and state legislatures unless a law clearly violates the Constitution is practicing
choices: executive privilege
judicial review
judicial activism
judicial restraint
questions.explanation: Deferring to elected branches is judicial restraint.
choiceExplanations: Executive privilege is a presidential claim, not a judicial approach.
Judicial review is the power itself, which restraint uses sparingly.
Activism is a greater willingness to overturn elected branches' decisions.

questions.prompt: Which is a way Congress can check the federal courts?
choices: Proposing a constitutional amendment to reverse a decision
Overruling a Supreme Court decision by a joint resolution
Ordering the Court to rehear a case it has already decided
Removing a justice by a simple majority vote in the House
questions.explanation: Congress can propose amendments (as with several decisions in the past), confirm or reject nominees, and change the courts' jurisdiction.
choiceExplanations: A resolution can't overrule a constitutional decision.
Congress can't order the Court to rehear cases.
Removal requires House impeachment and conviction by two-thirds of the Senate.

questions.prompt: The Environmental Protection Agency is an example of
choices: an independent executive agency
a congressional committee
a cabinet department
a government corporation like the Postal Service
questions.explanation: The EPA is an independent executive agency outside the cabinet departments.
choiceExplanations: Congressional committees are part of the legislative branch.
Cabinet departments include agencies such as the Department of Education.
Government corporations, such as the Postal Service, sell services; the EPA regulates.

questions.prompt: Congress passes a law requiring cleaner air but leaves the specific limits on pollutants to an agency. This illustrates
choices: judicial review
delegated rulemaking authority
an executive agreement with Congress
a congressional veto
questions.explanation: Congress delegates authority, and the agency uses discretion to write detailed regulations.
choiceExplanations: Judicial review is a power of the courts.
Executive agreements are made by the president with other nations, not with Congress.
No veto is involved in delegating authority.

questions.prompt: An iron triangle is a relationship among
choices: the president, the Senate, and the Supreme Court's justices
a state government, a city, and a federal court
voters, political parties, and the news media
an agency, a congressional committee, and an interest group
questions.explanation: Iron triangles form among an agency, the committee that oversees it, and the group it affects, all with shared interests.
choiceExplanations: Those are constitutional actors, not the triangle's members.
These are levels of government and a court, not an iron triangle.
These are actors in elections, not policy subsystems.

questions.prompt: Which action is the clearest example of Congress holding the bureaucracy accountable?
choices: An interest group sues the agency in federal court
A committee holds hearings and then cuts the agency's budget
A federal court rules that an agency rule exceeds its legal authority
The president appoints a new head of the agency
questions.explanation: Oversight hearings and the power of the purse are Congress's main accountability tools.
choiceExplanations: A lawsuit is an outside challenge, not congressional oversight.
Court rulings are a judicial check.
Appointments are a presidential check, not a congressional one.
